name: Marina Bay Sands
label: Marina Bay Sands
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Marina Bay Sands'.

text.description:
Marina Bay Sands is the three-tower resort on the edge of Marina Bay, and it is probably the easiest building in Singapore to recognise. The three hotel towers are topped by a long platform called the Sands Skypark. That long platform gives you a strong silhouette against the sky, and it is the main reason the building photographs so well from the ground. The architect, Moshe Safdie, has said the design was first inspired by decks of cards.

A few facts help you read what you are looking at. The Skypark is 340 metres long and holds a 150-metre infinity pool. It sits on a cantilevered platform that overhangs the north tower by 66.5 metres. The hotel has 1,850 rooms, and the resort and Skypark officially opened on 23 and 24 June 2010. The ArtScience Museum is part of the same complex.

The towers are huge, so you will not fit everything in from close range unless you use the ultra-wide lens. If you want a tidier composition, step back until the whole building fits, and keep your phone level so the towers do not lean. Walk around a little too, because the building looks quite different from each side.
text.geographic_location: Marina Bay Sands is on the waterfront of Marina Bay in Singapore, right beside Bayfront MRT station.
text.directions_text: For the photo, go to the Fullerton side of Marina Bay, next to Merlion Park. The nearest station is Raffles Place MRT, about 430 m from the phone icon; walk towards the waterfront. The phone icon on the map is about 740 m north-west of Marina Bay Sands, across the water. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there. To visit the hotel itself, use Bayfront MRT station (MRT Circle Line and MRT Downtown Line), right beside it.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: From across the bay the hotel is about 740 m away. Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the three towers, the Skypark and their reflection in Marina Bay. Then use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the towers and the Skypark. The ultra-wide (0.5x) makes the hotel look small from here, so use it only if you want lots of water and sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 740 m north-west of the subject, on Fullerton Promenade at the water's edge (the phone icon on the map), and face south-east across Marina Bay. From here the three towers and the Skypark line up across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the far shoreline level. Put the waterline on the lower third so the reflection fills the bottom of the frame and the towers rise above it. Leave a little space on each side so the Skypark is not cut off.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the towers to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the lit windows do not burn out. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a railing to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early evening, around dusk, is a good bet because the sky and the building lights can both show up. In low light, use night mode and brace your elbows against a wall or rail to keep the shot steady.

text.access_note: The area around the resort can be photographed from outside, but the Skypark, pool and some other parts may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The sky and the building lights both tend to show well in the early evening around dusk.
From the stand-here point the towers are close enough that the ultra-wide lens is useful.
Tilting the phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean inwards.

name: Sentosa
label: Sentosa
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9574725: large area 'Sentosa' (5275 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: An island resort: the pin is at its centre.

text.description: Sentosa is the island resort just off Singapore's southern coast, and it makes an easy, relaxed stop for a few phone photos. The subject here is the island generally rather than one building, so think of this as a scene-setting shot: water, greenery and the feel of a holiday island. The island is separated from the main island by Keppel Harbour, and it once served as a British military base and later a Japanese prisoner-of-war camp. It was renamed Sentosa in the early 1970s, a Malay word meaning peace and tranquility. Today it is a tourist destination with a 2.5 km sheltered beach, Fort Siloso, a cable car network, hotels and Resorts World Sentosa, and it is said to receive up to 25 million visitors a year. That mix gives you plenty of variety: open sea and sky for wide views, and palm trees, paths and people for lively foreground detail. Start at the phone icon on the map, then take a few steps either way to find a clear view without railings or signs cutting across the frame. Keep the horizon level using your gridlines, and include something close by, such as a tree branch or a path edge, to give the picture depth. If the place is busy, wait a moment for a gap in the crowd, or shoot a little higher to keep the sky as the main feature.
text.geographic_location: Sentosa sits off the southern coast of Singapore's main island, across the channel of Keppel Harbour and next to the smaller island of Pulau Brani.
text.directions_text: The nearest stations are on the Sentosa Express (monorail): Resorts World station is about 21 minutes on foot from the Sentosa point on the map, in a straight line, with the Sentosa point lying to the south-east of it. Imbiah station is about 22 minutes on foot, and the Sentosa point also lies to the south-east of it. The phone icon on the map is about 160 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the sweep of water, shoreline and sky. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single detail such as a boat, a tree or a distant building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 160 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line rather than in the middle. Add something close to you, such as leaves or a path edge, to give the picture depth. For a quick extra shot, try a panorama, moving the phone slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main subject to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Try a Live Photo if there is movement such as waves or passers-by, so you can pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Midday sun can look harsh and flat, so keep the exposure slider handy.

text.access_note: Sentosa is a managed island resort, so check current access details before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning and late afternoon usually give softer light and are often quieter than midday.

name: Gardens by the Bay and the Supertree Grove
label: Gardens by the Bay
camera_source: Commons cluster (166 photos). Moved 42 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 50 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/171142595: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Flower Dome' (192 m across).

text.description:
Gardens by the Bay is a 105-hectare waterfront park next to Marina Reservoir, and the Supertree Grove sits in its largest section, Bay South Garden. That garden opened on 29 June 2012 and was designed by Grant Associates. Its plan takes its idea from an orchid, with the Supertrees placed as the 'blooms' where paths and links meet. The Supertrees also do a job: they help vent hot air and cool circulated water for the two big glass conservatories, the Flower Dome and the Cloud Forest, nearby.

The grove photographs well because the tall, tree-like structures give you strong vertical shapes against open sky, and the paths around them lead the eye upwards. Gardens by the Bay is a popular attraction, with over 50 million visitors by 2018, so expect other people in your frames and treat them as scale rather than a problem.

Hold the phone upright, keep the grid lines on, and line the tallest trunks up with a vertical grid line so they don't lean. Take one wide shot from the marked point, then walk closer and shoot straight up for a more abstract picture. Check your lens is clean before you start, as humid air can leave a faint film on it.
text.geographic_location: The map's subject point is the middle of the Flower Dome, in Bay South Garden, part of Gardens by the Bay in Singapore's Central Region, next to Marina Reservoir and the Marina South area. The Supertree Grove is in the same garden.
text.directions_text: From Gardens by the Bay MRT station (MRT Thomson–East Coast Line), the middle of the Flower Dome is about 686 metres away to the north-west, about 11 minutes on foot. From Bayfront MRT station (MRT Circle Line and MRT Downtown Line) it is about 677 metres to the north-east, about 11 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole grove in from the marked point. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view with less edge stretching. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the tops of individual Supertrees.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. You are far enough back to see the Supertrees as a group rather than one at a time.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tallest trunks up with a vertical line so they stay straight. Keep the phone level and avoid tilting it upwards from the marked point. For a second shot, walk in close, point the phone up, and use the Supertrees' shapes as a pattern. Wait a moment for people to move through the foreground, or include them to show size.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the structures to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. If you shoot after dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a railing to keep the phone still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, and the hour around dusk suits the grove best as the sky darkens. Check the official site for any evening light displays.

text.access_note: The Gardens are a large managed park, and some attractions such as the conservatories may need tickets or have set hours, so check the official site before you go.

name: Raffles Hotel
label: Raffles Hotel
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/11517501222: the OpenStreetMap point 'Raffles Hotel'.

text.description: Raffles Hotel is one of Singapore's best-known old buildings, and a good subject for a phone camera because the long, formal frontage fits neatly into a single frame. The Sarkies Brothers opened it on 1 December 1887 with just ten rooms, in a building that began as a beach house. The main building you see today was designed by Regent Alfred John Bidwell and finished in 1899. It was reportedly the first hotel in the region with electric lights. The hotel was gazetted as a national monument in 1987. After a long renovation it reopened on 1 August 2019. It is also the place where the Singapore Sling cocktail was invented, at the Long Bar. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m west of the subject. That distance lets you capture the whole frontage without tilting the phone upwards, which keeps the vertical lines straight. Wait for a gap in passers-by and traffic before you shoot. Then take a second, closer picture of a single detail such as an entrance, a window or the signage. Together the wide shot and the detail make a pleasant pair. If you want to photograph inside, such as the lobby or arcade, check the official site before you go, as rules for non-guests may apply.
text.geographic_location: Raffles Hotel is at 1 Beach Road in Singapore, a short walk from Esplanade MRT station and City Hall MRT station.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Esplanade MRT station (MRT Circle Line), about 3 minutes on foot, with the hotel to the north-west. City Hall MRT station (MRT East-West Line and MRT North-South Line) is also close, about 5 minutes on foot, with the hotel to the north-east. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole frontage from where you stand. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move much closer, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as signs, windows or rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. The building should sit roughly in the middle of the frame, with space around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's horizontal edges with them. Hold the phone level and at chest height to keep verticals upright. Leave a little foreground, such as a path or greenery, to give a sense of scale. Then step closer and use 2x or more for one detail shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the walls do not wash out. In the evening, try night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to early evening is likely to give the best light on the frontage, as the sun will be behind you in the west. Early morning tends to be quieter if you want fewer people in the shot.

text.access_note: The hotel is a private, working hotel and national monument, so access to the interior and arcade may be limited; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The stand-here point is west of the hotel, so in the late afternoon and early evening the sun is behind the photographer and lights the frontage.
Early morning is usually quieter than the rest of the day.

name: Sri Mariamman Temple
label: Sri Mariamman
camera_source: Commons cluster (7 photos), weak. Moved 6 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 30 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/300380459: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sri Mariamman Temple' (54 m across).

text.description:
Sri Mariamman Temple is Singapore's first and oldest Hindu temple, and it stands out among the shophouses of Chinatown. Its main draw for a phone camera is the gopuram, the entrance tower above South Bridge Road. It has six tiers of plaster sculptures of Hindu deities and other figures, all painted in bright colours. Each tier is a little smaller than the one below, which makes the tower look taller than it is. That gives you a strong, simple shape to build a photo around, and plenty of small detail for close-ups.

The temple was founded in 1827 by Naraina Pillai, a government clerk who became a successful businessman. The oldest parts of the present brick structure date from 1843, and the six-tiered tower you see today was built in 1925. It was restored in the 1960s. The temple became a National Monument in 1973.

For a good overall shot, use the phone icon on the map. From there the temple is about 45 metres to the west, far enough back to fit much of the tower into the frame. Keep your phone upright so the tower fills the picture, and leave a little sky above the top tier. Then move closer and use the zoom to pick out single figures and the flanking sculptures. The temple is a working place of worship, so be discreet, keep out of the way of people praying, and ask before photographing worshippers up close.
text.geographic_location: The temple is on South Bridge Road in the Chinatown district of downtown Singapore, at about 1.28268° N, 103.84521° E. Pagoda Street and Temple Street run along its sides. Chinatown MRT station and Maxwell MRT station are both within a few minutes' walk.
text.directions_text: Take the MRT Downtown Line or the MRT North East Line to Chinatown MRT station. The temple is about 3 minutes on foot from there (about 209 metres to the south-east). If you arrive at Maxwell MRT station on the MRT Thomson–East Coast Line, the temple is about 5 minutes on foot (about 301 metres to the north-east). From either station, head towards South Bridge Road and look for the tall coloured tower. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand to take in most of the tower. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole tower and the street in front of it. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the painted figures on the upper tiers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. For close-ups of the sculptures, walk nearer along the street, but stay clear of the entrance so people can pass.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and turn on gridlines. Put the centre of the tower on the middle vertical line and keep the sides as straight as you can. Leave a little sky above the top tier. If you use 0.5x, stand square-on to the tower, because tilting the phone makes the sides lean inwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out the bright colours. For detail shots, zoom in and tap on a single sculpture to focus.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day usually means fewer people and softer light, and late afternoon can also work well. Midday sun can be harsh on the colours, so check your photos and adjust the exposure slider if needed.

text.access_note: The temple is a place of worship and a National Monument, so visiting rules, dress expectations and photography permission inside may apply: check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning usually has fewer visitors and softer light than midday.
Midday sun can be harsh on bright colours.

name: Merlion Park
label: Merlion
camera_source: Commons cluster (8 photos), weak. Moved 3 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 40 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/182819157: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Merlion Fountain' (4 m across).

text.description:
The Merlion is Singapore's official mascot: a creature with a lion's head and a fish's body. The lion recalls the name Singapura, meaning 'lion city', and the fish recalls the old fishing village of Temasek. This statue stands 8.6 metres high and was finished in 1972. It was moved in 2002 to its current spot on a promontory in front of the Fullerton Hotel, near the mouth of the Singapore River. Its water spout is the part everyone wants in the frame.

It photographs well because the setting does a lot of the work. A viewing deck stretches out over the river, so you can get the statue with the water and the city skyline behind it. The statue faces east, so from the phone icon on the map you will mostly see it from the side, with the spout in profile. That makes a pleasing, slightly different shot from the usual straight-on view.

The phone icon on the map is about 40 m south of the subject. From there you can fit the whole figure and some skyline into one frame without squeezing into the crowd at the front rail. Take a few frames at different distances rather than just one. The spot is popular, so expect other visitors in the frame, and be patient for a gap. Wipe your phone lens before you start, as the spray and humidity can leave a faint haze on it.
text.geographic_location: Merlion Park sits on the Marina Bay waterfront in Singapore's central area, in front of the Fullerton Hotel and close to the mouth of the Singapore River.
text.directions_text: Take the MRT to Raffles Place MRT station (MRT East-West Line or MRT North-South Line). The park is about 7 minutes on foot from the station, to the north-east. The phone icon on the map is about 40 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue and the water. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the skyline, or to 2x if you want a tighter shot of the head and spout.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 40 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From here you see the statue from the side, with the spout in profile.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the statue on one of the vertical lines, leaving space on the side it faces. Keep the horizon level. Hold the phone low and tilt up slightly if you want the statue to stand out against the sky, but avoid tilting too far or the figure will look squashed.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky and water don't wash out the stone. Try a Live Photo to catch the moving water from the spout, and use night mode after dark, resting your elbows on the rail to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, and the hour around sunset or just after dark often gives softer light and a lit skyline. Midday sun is harsh and the crowds are at their biggest.

text.access_note: This is a public waterfront park with a viewing deck, but check the official site before you go in case of maintenance or temporary restrictions.

name: Singapore Botanic Gardens
label: Botanic Gardens
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/47257476: large area 'Singapore Botanic Gardens' (1929 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description: Singapore Botanic Gardens is a large tropical garden on the edge of the Orchard Road shopping district, and it is a calm change from the city streets nearby. It is one of only three gardens to be named a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the only tropical one. The present gardens date from 1859, and the layout today still follows the English landscape style planned by Lawrence Niven, with winding paths, open lawns and groups of trees. Swan Lake was dug out in 1866, so water and reflections are part of the scene. The grounds cover about 82 hectares, and the longest stretch from north to south is around 2.5 km, so you will not see everything in one visit. That is useful for photographers, because you can choose one or two views and take your time over them. Wide lawns and big trees suit sweeping landscape shots, while the National Orchid Garden inside the grounds is good for close-ups of flowers. Give yourself time to look around before you shoot, as the best frames are often a few steps off the main path. Look for a clear foreground, such as a path or a patch of lawn, and let the trees fill the background. Keep your phone lens clean, because humid air and the odd shower can leave marks. Check the official Singapore Botanic Gardens website for current entry details before you go.
text.geographic_location: The gardens lie in central Singapore, at the edge of the Orchard Road shopping district, in the Tanglin area, at about 1.3151° N, 103.8162° E.
text.directions_text: Take the MRT to Botanic Gardens MRT station, which is on the MRT Circle Line and the MRT Downtown Line. From there the gardens are about 13 minutes on foot (about 813 m), lying to the south of the station. Allow a few extra minutes to reach it once you are inside. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for natural-looking views of lawns and paths. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want to fit in a wide stretch of grass and tall trees. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as leaves, flowers or distant trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 120 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon or tree line on the upper third, leaving the lower two-thirds for lawn or path. A curving path in the foreground leads the eye into the picture. If you use the ultra-wide, keep the edges clear of passers-by, as people can look stretched there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the greenest part of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so bright sky does not wash out the leaves. For flowers, try portrait mode or the telephoto, and hold still for a second after tapping to focus.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Midday sun makes harsh shadows under the trees.

text.access_note: The gardens are a public park. Check the official Singapore Botanic Gardens website for current entry details before you go.

name: Singapore Flyer
label: Singapore Flyer
camera_source: Commons cluster (9 photos), weak. Moved 73 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 160 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/230082125: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Singapore Flyer' (155 m across).

text.description:
The Singapore Flyer is a giant observation wheel in Marina Centre, along the Marina Promenade, and it is one of the easiest landmarks in the city to spot from a distance. It opened officially on 15 April 2008 and stands 165 metres tall. On completion that made it the tallest Ferris wheel in the world, though taller ones have since been built. Its 28 air-conditioned capsules are mounted on the outside of the rim, so the wheel keeps a clean, open outline against the sky, which suits a phone photo. A full turn takes about 32 minutes.

From this distance the wheel is so large that you will struggle to fit all of it into the frame with anything but the widest lens. That is useful, because you can pick between a full view of the wheel with some sky around it and a closer, tighter shot of the rim and capsules. Look for a foreground such as a railing, a tree or a passer-by to give the picture a sense of scale. Keep your phone upright for the full height of the wheel, or turn it sideways if you want to include more of the surroundings. If you plan to ride, the capsules are air-conditioned. The views from the top are worth saving your battery for.
text.geographic_location: The Singapore Flyer is in the Downtown Core district, in Marina Centre, along the Marina Promenade. Its centre is at about 1.2894° N, 103.8631° E, and the wheel is roughly 155 m across.
text.directions_text: Start at Promenade MRT station, which is on the MRT Circle Line and the MRT Downtown Line. From there the Flyer is to the south-east, about 7 minutes on foot (roughly 450 m in a straight line). The phone icon on the map is about 160 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole wheel into the frame from where you stand. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view with a little sky around it. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the capsules along the rim.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 160 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. If the whole wheel does not fit, take a few steps back rather than tilting the phone upwards, which makes the wheel lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the wheel's centre near one of the vertical lines, with the base of the wheel on the lower line. For the full height, hold the phone upright. Include a person, tree or railing in the foreground to show how big the wheel is. For a closer shot, use telephoto on the rim and capsules.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the wheel to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on a railing or wall to keep the phone steady. Take a few shots, since the capsules move.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and a calmer sky. After dark the wheel should be lit, which suits night mode. Check the weather first, since cloud or haze can flatten the view.

text.access_note: The area around the wheel can be photographed from outside, but rides are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

The wheel is lit up after dark.

name: Little India and the Tan Teng Niah house
label: Little India
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/19910162: large area 'Little India' (1081 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Little India is the neighbourhood east of the Singapore River, across from Chinatown and north of Kampong Glam. It is a lively mix of shophouses, markets, flower stalls, temples and spice and grocery shops. The House of Tan Teng Niah is one of the best-known buildings in the area, and it makes a good first stop for a short photo walk. The streets are busy with signs, garlands, shopfronts and people, so there is plenty to frame, from wide street scenes to small details.

The area has been a conservation area since 7 July 1989, and many Indian businesses and traditional trades are still found here. It is also known for markets such as Tekka and for festivals through the year, including Deepavali and Thaipusam. Shophouses along Kerbau Road are home to the Little India Arts Belt.

For photos, think in layers. Start with a wide view of the street, then move in on a doorway, a flower stall or a row of hanging garlands. Walk a little between shots, because the best angle is often a few steps away. Keep your phone ready but be polite: ask before photographing people up close, especially at shops and places of worship. Keep the pavement clear for others while you line up a picture. The phone icon on the map is a short walk from the subject, so you can take your time and choose your angle.
text.geographic_location: Little India is in central Singapore, east of the Singapore River and north of Kampong Glam, close to Serangoon Road and the Tekka area. Rochor MRT station and Little India MRT station are both within a short walk.

Try portrait mode for details like flowers or garlands. Avoid zooming past 5x, as the picture will get soft.

name: ArtScience Museum
label: ArtScience Museum
camera_source: Commons cluster (4 photos), weak. Moved 42 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 580 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14314416: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'ArtScience Museum' (122 m across).

text.description:
The ArtScience Museum sits on the waterfront of Marina Bay Sands, and its shape is the reason to photograph it. The building is said to recall an open lotus flower, with a round base in the middle and ten curving extensions, or "fingers", reaching out from it. Moshe Safdie designed it, and the outer skin is fibre-reinforced plastic over a steel lattice. The pale, sculpted form stands out clearly against sky and water, so it makes a tidy subject even for a quick snap.

The museum opened on 17 February 2011 and is the largest private museum in Singapore. Inside, it mostly shows touring exhibitions, plus a permanent show called Future World made with the art collective teamLab. Skylights at the fingertips let daylight into the galleries, which explains the openings you can see in the roof shapes.

The phone icon on the map is about 580 m north-west of the subject. That distance suits a phone well, because you can include the curved fingers and the surroundings without any distortion from standing too close. Keep the horizon level, using the gridlines, and let the water take up the lower part of the picture. If other people wander into the foreground, wait a moment or take a few frames. Wipe the lens before you start, as a smudge shows up badly against a bright sky.
text.geographic_location: The museum is part of the Marina Bay Sands resort on the Marina Bay waterfront, in the Downtown Core of Singapore's Central Area.
text.directions_text: Take the MRT to Bayfront MRT station (MRT Circle Line or MRT Downtown Line); the museum is to the north, about 7 minutes on foot. Once there, face south-east to see the museum ahead of you. The phone icon on the map is about 580 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole building and the water. If your phone has a telephoto lens (2x-5x), try 2x or 3x to fill more of the frame with the lotus shape. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground, as it makes the museum look small and far away.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 580 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Stay put rather than walking closer, because this distance keeps the full shape in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Place the museum off-centre using the gridlines, with the horizon on the lower third line. Include some water or sky so the curved fingers have room around them. Keep the phone level so the building does not appear to lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the museum to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the pale building keeps its detail. At dusk, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on a rail or wall to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk usually gives softer light and a more colourful sky, and the area tends to be lit after dark. Early morning is often calmer if you want fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the waterfront, but entry to the museum and its exhibitions is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Chinatown
label: Chinatown
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/19910170: large area 'Chinatown' (1631 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Chinatown is a whole neighbourhood rather than a single building, and it rewards slow wandering with a phone in hand. It sits in Singapore's Central Area and is made up of five precincts: Kreta Ayer, Ann Siang/Club Street, Telok Ayer, Tanjong Pagar/Duxton and Bukit Pasoh. These were built up at different times, from the 1820s to the 1920s, which is why the streets vary so much in character. It is best known for its rows of shophouses, traditional markets and religious landmarks such as Thian Hock Keng Temple and Sri Mariamman Temple.

The layout goes back to the 1822 town plan drawn up under Sir Stamford Raffles, which set aside the land southwest of the Singapore River for Chinese migrants. That plan also required the covered walkway along the front of buildings known as the five-foot way. Those shaded arcades and repeating shopfronts give you natural lines and frames for photos. The Malay name Kreta Ayer means "water cart", a reminder of how water was once delivered here.

For photos, look for streets where shophouse facades run away from you in a long perspective, with signs, lanterns and shopfronts adding colour. Keep people in the frame to show the scale and the activity. The phone icon on the map is a short walk from the subject and gives you a view back towards the main streets. Expect pedestrians and delivery traffic, so take a few frames and pick the cleanest. Wipe your lens before you start, as humid air and fingerprints soften phone shots.
text.geographic_location: Chinatown lies in the Outram district in Singapore's Central Area, on the southwest side of the Singapore River. It is right beside Chinatown MRT station.
text.directions_text: Start at Chinatown MRT station, which is served by the MRT Downtown Line and the MRT North East Line. The subject is about 1 minute on foot from the station, to the south. If you prefer, Maxwell MRT station on the MRT Thomson–East Coast Line is about 6 minutes on foot from the subject, which lies to the north of that station. The phone icon on the map is about 4 minutes on foot from the subject, and from there you look north-west towards it. The phone icon on the map is about 220 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for narrow streets and tall shophouse rows, then switch to the default lens (1x) for most street scenes. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out signs, lanterns and rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 220 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up a street edge or the five-foot way arcade with one of the lines so the buildings do not lean. Place a bright shopfront or lantern off-centre, and wait for a passer-by to walk into the lower third for scale. Keep your phone level to avoid converging verticals, which are more obvious with the ultra-wide.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-tone wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so bright signs and lit windows do not burn out. Try portrait mode on a shopkeeper or a detail such as a lantern, but ask first if a person is close. After dark, night mode helps, but hold the phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter for clean street views. Late afternoon into evening gives softer light and lit signs, though it is busier.

name: Fort Canning Park and the Tree Tunnel
label: Fort Canning
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/9794258968: the OpenStreetMap point 'Fort Canning Hill'.

text.description: Fort Canning Park covers a green hill just on the edge of Singapore's busy downtown. The hill is about 48 metres high, which makes it the highest point within walking distance of the civic district. It has a long story. Malays called it Bukit Larangan, or Forbidden Hill, and it was said to be where ancient kings were laid to rest. In 1819 William Farquhar raised the Union Jack on the summit. Stamford Raffles later built his residence here, and the hill was renamed Fort Canning in 1861, when a military fort was built. A cemetery once existed on the slopes, with a Gothic gateway built in 1846 to enclose it. Today it is a place for walks, concerts and exhibitions. It photographs well because the park's shaded paths and old trees give you a leafy, calm scene so close to the towers and streets of the centre. A tree-lined path with light coming through the leaves makes a natural frame. Walk slowly, look up as well as ahead, and take a few different versions of the same view. Wipe your lens before you start, as park humidity can leave a faint smear that makes pictures look hazy. If the path is busy, wait for a gap rather than rushing, and keep to the side so other walkers can pass.
text.geographic_location: Fort Canning Park is on Fort Canning Hill in Singapore's Central Area, next to the downtown business district. Fort Canning MRT station is about 275 m to the south-west of the hill's centre point, and Clarke Quay MRT station is about 533 m to the south of it.

Once in the park, follow the paths towards the phone icon on the map, which is a short walk north of the hill's centre point. The phone icon on the map is about 200 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to squeeze the trees together and pick out details such as a single trunk or the texture of the leaves.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 200 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the path along the centre or one third line so it leads into the picture. Hold the phone low and tilt it up a little to catch more of the leaves overhead. Wait for a gap in the walkers, or include one person for scale. Keep the vertical lines of the trunks straight by lining them up with the gridlines.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the path to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright patches of sky don't wash out. If the light is patchy, try a Live Photo and choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light under the trees and fewer people on the paths. Midday light can be harsh and patchy.

name: Buddha Tooth Relic Temple
label: Buddha Tooth Relic
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3756800538: the OpenStreetMap point 'Buddha Tooth Relic Museum'.

text.description:
The Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum sits in Chinatown and is built in the style of the Tang dynasty. That gives it a very different look from the older, Southern Chinese-style temples nearby. The design went through nine proposals before it was settled, and the abbot turned down anything that felt too contemporary for Chinatown. The result is a large, symmetrical building with deep red doors, sweeping roofs and gold details, which suits a phone camera well.

The entrance gateway, the Shanmen, has three big red lacquered doors fitted with gilt bronze studs and lion door knockers. This is the part to look for in your frame. The centre door is normally kept for important guests, so photograph it from outside rather than walking through it. Inside, the temple is named for a tooth relic that visitors can see on the 4th floor. The tooth measures 7.5 cm. There are also several halls and a museum with 278 exhibits.

For the best photo of the building, stay at the phone icon on the map. The temple is only about 8 m away, so use the ultra-wide lens if you want the whole front in a single shot. Keep an eye on passers-by in the foreground, and wait a few seconds for a clear gap. If you go inside, look for signs about where photography is allowed and keep your phone lowered in prayer areas.
text.geographic_location: The temple is in the Chinatown district of Singapore, about 127 m from Maxwell MRT station and about 338 m from Chinatown MRT station.
text.directions_text: Take the MRT Thomson–East Coast Line to Maxwell MRT station. The temple is to the north-east, about 127 m away, which is about 2 minutes on foot. If you arrive on the MRT Downtown Line or the MRT North East Line at Chinatown MRT station, the temple is to the south, about 338 m away, which is about 5 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade from where you stand. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are too close or the building will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the roof edges, the gold details and the red doors.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. At this distance, use the ultra-wide lens if the whole front will not fit in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the centre of the Shanmen with the middle vertical line. Keep the phone level so the roof lines stay straight. Use the red doors and gold roof as the main colours, and include a little sky above the roof. If people are passing in front, wait for a gap or let one person into the shot for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red doors to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the reds and golds stay rich and the sky does not wash out. If you shoot at 0.5x, keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where lines can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kind to the red and gold. If you shoot after dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or rail.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship and museum, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements, any dress code and rules on photography inside.

name: Haji Lane and Kampong Glam
label: Haji Lane
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5639900: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Haji Lane is a narrow street of old shophouses in the Kampong Glam neighbourhood, now known for small independent shops, cafés and bars. It photographs well because everything is close together: rows of narrow, colourful building fronts, shop signs and café tables, with people passing through. It feels lively and a bit cramped, and that is the picture to go for.

The street's story adds interest. It takes its name from the Arab pilgrim-brokers who once arranged the haj for Muslims in Singapore and from nearby islands such as Java. From the 1800s into the 1960s, many of the shophouses were lodgings for pilgrims, who worked nearby as hawkers to save for the rest of their journey. In the 1960s and 70s the buildings became homes for poorer Malay families, and after the 1970s many stood empty or were used for storage. The shops and cafés you see today are a much later chapter.

For your phone, think in layers: shopfronts, signs and upper-floor windows give you plenty to frame. Take a wide view of the lane first, then move closer for details such as a doorway, a hanging sign or a café corner. Keep an eye on the edges of the frame, because in a tight street the buildings can lean inward if you tilt the phone upwards. Be polite with people in shops and cafés, and wait a moment for a clear gap in the foot traffic if you want an emptier shot.
text.geographic_location: Haji Lane is in the Kampong Glam neighbourhood, in the Bugis area of central Singapore. It lies about 5 minutes' walk east of Bugis MRT station.
text.directions_text: Start at Bugis MRT station (MRT Downtown Line and MRT East-West Line). The lane is about 293 m away to the east, which is about 5 minutes on foot. From Nicoll Highway MRT station (MRT Circle Line) it is about 523 m to the west, about 8 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lane as you see it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too tight to fit the buildings in, and to telephoto (2x) to pick out signs and details without walking into other people's shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the buildings with them so they don't lean. Use the shopfronts on both sides as a frame leading into the picture. Then step closer for one detail shot, such as a doorway, a sign or a window.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the building fronts to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so signs and sky are not washed out. Portrait mode suits a café table or a single object. Live Photos can help catch a moment when people walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day the lane is usually quieter and easier to photograph. Late afternoon can give softer light. In the evening the shop lights and signs add colour, so try night mode, keeping your arms steady.

text.access_note: It is an ordinary public street; individual shops, cafés and bars set their own rules, so check the official site or ask on the spot before you go in.

name: Clarke Quay
label: Clarke Quay
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Clarke Quay'.

text.description:
Clarke Quay is a stretch of the Singapore River lined with restored warehouses, now home to restaurants, bars and nightlife. It was once a busy trading quay, where bumboats crowded the water edge and goods were carried upstream to the warehouses. Cargo moved to a new port at Pasir Panjang, the river was cleaned up between 1977 and 1987, and the quay was reborn as a leisure district, with Clarke Quay Festival Village opening on 10 December 1993. British firm Alsop Architects redesigned the shophouse facades and riverfront from 2003. The area reopened in April 2024 as CQ @ Clarke Quay after an upgrade that included the Angel Canopies, the shading structures over the inner streets.

It photographs well because there is plenty to look at: the warehouse blocks, the river, refurbished Chinese junks moored as floating pubs and restaurants, and a new mural by Yip Yew Chong and tobyato on the Block B warehouses. The canopies and the colourful buildings give you strong shapes and bold colour, especially once the lights come on.

For phone photos, start at the phone icon on the map and look west towards the quay. Stand back from the water edge so you can include the buildings and their reflections. Keep an eye on people walking through, and take a few frames so you can pick the one with the best gaps in the crowd.
text.geographic_location: Clarke Quay sits on the Singapore River, upstream from Boat Quay and the river mouth, in the Singapore River Planning Area. Clarke Quay MRT station (MRT North East Line) is nearby, about 150 m away.
text.directions_text: Start from Clarke Quay MRT station (MRT North East Line). The quay is about 150 m to the north-west, which is about 2 minutes on foot. Alternatively, Fort Canning MRT station (MRT Downtown Line) is about 5 minutes on foot, with the quay to the south-east. The phone icon on the map is about 130 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of warehouses, canopies and river. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the buildings and boats. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out details such as the mural, the junks or the canopy shapes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 130 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the river or the building edges with the horizontal lines so the scene looks level. Include some water in the foreground for reflections, and the canopies or warehouse facades behind. Wait for a gap in the people walking past if you want a cleaner frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright part of the scene to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so lit signs and lights do not look washed out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early evening, around dusk, when the lights come on and there is still some colour in the sky. Daytime is better for the architecture and the mural.

name: Sultan Mosque
label: Sultan Mosque
camera_source: Commons cluster (11 photos). Moved 6 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 30 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/155990076: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Masjid Sultan' (83 m across).

text.description: The Sultan Mosque is the best-known mosque in Singapore and the centrepiece of the Kampong Glam district. Its two gold-coloured onion domes and the pair of tall minarets on the Muscat Street side make a strong, easily recognised shape, and the gold stands out well against a blue sky. The mosque was first completed in 1826, then rebuilt in stages between 1925 and 1931 and finished in 1932 to a design by the Irish architect Denis Santry. It became a national monument in 1975. One small detail is worth a close-up: the bases of the domes are decorated with the cut ends of glass bottles, collected from poorer members of the community during the rebuilding. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m south-east of the subject. From there you can capture the domes and the main facade together, with room for a few people in the foreground to show the scale. The area around the mosque is a good place to wander afterwards, so take a few frames from different angles. Keep your phone steady against the light and give the building a little space at the top of the frame so the domes are not cut off. The grounds are open to visitors of different faiths, but check the official site before you go for current visiting arrangements and dress guidance.
text.geographic_location: The Sultan Mosque stands in the Kampong Glam district of Rochor, in central Singapore (about 1.3022° N, 103.8590° E), on the Muscat Street side of the old Malay quarter and close to North Bridge Road.
text.directions_text: Start from Bugis MRT station (MRT Downtown Line or MRT East-West Line) and head north-east towards Kampong Glam; the mosque is about 364 m away, about 6 minutes on foot. Jalan Besar MRT station (MRT Downtown Line) is another option: the mosque lies to its south-east, about 533 m away, or about 9 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building, then switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit the minarets and domes in. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the domes, the crescent-and-star emblems and the minaret tops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. If you want more of the facade, move a few steps along the pavement rather than zooming in from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the minarets parallel to the edges of the screen. Hold the phone level so the building does not lean. Leave a little sky above the domes and include a bit of foreground, such as the railings or a passer-by, for scale. For a close-up, use zoom on the gold domes and the decorated bases.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the gold domes and bright sky do not wash out. Keep the phone steady with both hands, and lean against a wall or railing if you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the gold domes and fewer people around. Midday is the harshest light for photos, so you may want to avoid it.

text.access_note: The grounds are open to visitors of different faiths, but it is a working place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and dress guidance.

name: National Gallery Singapore
label: National Gallery
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4759240362: the OpenStreetMap point 'National Gallery Singapore'.

text.description: National Gallery Singapore fills two grand old civic buildings, the former Supreme Court and the former City Hall, which face the Padang in the Civic District. They are joined by bridges and a newer basement level, and together they make the largest museum in Singapore, with more than 9,000 artworks of Singaporean and Southeast Asian art. For a phone photographer the appeal is the mix of styles. The City Hall building went up between 1926 and 1929. The Supreme Court building opened on 3 August 1939 and has Corinthian and Ionic columns, sculpted panels and a central domed rotunda. Both are national monuments, so the stonework is the star outside. The gallery opened to the public on 24 November 2015. The frontage is wide and the columns repeat in neat rows, which gives you strong lines and a good sense of scale. Stand back far enough to fit the whole front in, then move closer for details such as column tops, carved panels and the pattern of windows. Keep people in the foreground for scale if you like, but check the edges so nobody is cut in half. Wipe your lens first, as phone lenses pick up fingerprints easily. If you want to go inside, restaurants, cafés and exhibitions are there, but access and any ticketing can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Singapore's Civic District, in the former Supreme Court and City Hall buildings that face the Padang. It is a short walk south-west of City Hall MRT station.
text.directions_text: Start at City Hall MRT station (MRT East-West Line or MRT North-South Line) and walk south-west; the gallery is about 321 m away, about 5 minutes on foot. Alternatively, start at Clarke Quay MRT station (MRT North East Line) and walk east; the gallery is about 563 m away, about 9 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full width of the frontage from close range. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome, carvings and column tops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the rows of columns with the vertical grid lines so the buildings do not lean. Include some open ground or sky for breathing space. For a second shot, step in and fill the frame with columns and windows for a pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the facade keeps its detail. If you use the ultra-wide, keep the buildings away from the edges of the frame, where lines can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stonework and fewer harsh shadows than midday.

text.access_note: The outside of the buildings can be photographed from the surrounding public areas, but entry to the galleries may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday.
The outside of the buildings can be photographed from the surrounding public areas.

text.description:
Cloud Forest sits inside Gardens by the Bay, at Marina South in Singapore's Central Region. It is a large structure that gives you plenty to photograph, and it works well on a phone because the subject is big and the shapes are clear.

From outside, look for the overall shape of the structure and how it sits within the gardens around it. Move along the paths and take a few frames from different spots rather than waiting for a single perfect position.

For practical advice, keep your phone lens clean, because humidity can leave a film on it. Wipe it with a soft cloth before you shoot. Include a person or a railing in some frames to show the scale. Try one wide shot of the whole scene, then a closer shot of a single detail such as a texture or a pattern. Take your time, as the best frames often come when the crowd thins for a moment. Entry arrangements can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Cloud Forest is in Gardens by the Bay, at Marina South in Singapore's Central Region.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Gardens by the Bay MRT station on the MRT Thomson–East Coast Line, about 9 minutes on foot (about 548 m), with Cloud Forest to the north-west of the station. You can also use Bayfront MRT station on the MRT Circle Line or MRT Downtown Line, about 13 minutes on foot (about 796 m), with Cloud Forest to the east of that station. Once you are inside Gardens by the Bay, follow the signs for Cloud Forest. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole structure into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for most of your shots. If your phone has telephoto/zoom (2x-5x), use it for details such as textures and patterns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Treat it as a starting point and then step back along the path until the whole structure fits in your frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edge of the structure with one of the vertical lines. Keep your phone level so the tall shapes do not lean. Add some foreground, such as leaves or a railing, to give the picture depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest or most important part of the scene to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and bright areas do not wash out. If the light is low, hold the phone steady with both hands or against a railing, and let night mode work if it switches on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when it is quieter if you can, as clear views are easier without crowds. Check the official site for current visiting times before you plan.

text.access_note: Cloud Forest may be a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Humidity can fog or smear a phone lens.
The area is usually busier at some times of day and quieter at others.

name: Helix Bridge
label: Helix Bridge
camera_source: Commons cluster (10 photos). Moved 136 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 140 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18007977: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Helix Bridge' (280 m across).

text.description:
The Helix Bridge is a pedestrian bridge across the Marina Bay waterfront, joining Marina Centre with Marina South. Its steel frame is built as two spiralling helices that wind around the walkway, so it looks like a twisting DNA strand. That repeating curved pattern is what makes it so easy to photograph. It gives you strong lines, a clear shape against the sky and plenty of depth in a single frame.

The bridge opened on 24 April 2010, but only half of it at first because building work was still going on at Marina Bay Sands. The whole bridge was open by 18 July 2010. It is made from about 650 tonnes of duplex stainless steel. Small coloured letters (c, g, a and t) are set into the structure and stand for the four bases of DNA. They light up in red and green at night, and lights also pick out the spiral.

Four viewing platforms along the bridge look over the skyline and the bay, so you can also photograph the city from the bridge itself. Start there for a full view of the spiral, then walk onto the bridge for close-up details of the steel and the lettering. Keep the lens clean, as a smudge shows badly on the bright lights at night. Allow a little time, because the light changes the look of the steel quite a lot.
text.geographic_location: The Helix Bridge is in the Marina Bay area of central Singapore. It links Marina Centre with Marina South, next to the bay and close to Marina Bay Sands.
text.directions_text: Take the MRT to Promenade MRT station, which is on the MRT Circle Line and the MRT Downtown Line. From there the bridge is to the south, about 10 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole spiral into one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as the lettering or a section of the steel curve.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. From here the whole bridge is in front of you. For close-ups, walk onto the bridge and use the viewing platforms.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the bridge's long axis with one of the lines so the spiral leads the eye into the frame. Crouch slightly and use the ultra-wide lens to stretch the curves. Try one shot from where you stand and another from a platform with the skyline behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights and steel do not burn out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against the railing, or brace your elbows against your body, until the shot finishes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around dusk and into the evening, when the bridge lights are on and the sky still has some colour.

text.access_note: The Helix Bridge is a public pedestrian bridge; check the official site before you go in case of any closures or events.
claims_not_in_sources: Dusk and early evening, when the sky still has some colour, is a good time to photograph the bridge.
Crouching and using the ultra-wide lens exaggerates the curves of the spiral.
The bridge is a public pedestrian route that can normally be walked without a ticket.

name: Henderson Waves
label: Henderson Waves
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q61356513: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Henderson Waves is a pedestrian bridge that carries the Southern Ridges walking trail over Henderson Road, linking the Mount Faber side of the trail with the rest of the ridges. Its curved wooden ribs rise and dip along the deck like a long ribbon, which gives you strong lines and a recognisable shape. The ribs are lit at night, so the bridge can look quite different after dark.

A few facts help with planning. The bridge is 274 m long and 8 m wide, and it sits 36 m above the road. It is the tallest pedestrian bridge in Singapore. It opened on 10 May 2008, after a design competition run by the Urban Redevelopment Authority, and the winning design came from RSP Architects Planners & Engineers with IJP Architects.

The phone icon on the map is about 560 m south-west of the subject. From here the bridge will look fairly small at the default lens (1x). Use zoom to bring it closer and fill the frame with the wavy ribs. Wait for a gap in passers-by if you want a clean shot, and take a few frames, since small changes in angle alter how the curves line up. If you walk onto the bridge itself, the same ribs make good foreground lines for a shot along the deck.
text.geographic_location: Henderson Waves is in the Southern Ridges area in the south of Singapore, where the trail crosses Henderson Road on the way towards Mount Faber.
text.directions_text: From Telok Blangah MRT station (MRT Circle Line), the bridge is about 877 m to the north-east, about 14 minutes on foot. From HarbourFront MRT station (MRT Circle Line and MRT North East Line), it is about 1,367 m to the north-west, about 22 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 560 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to see the bridge in its surroundings. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the curved ribs closer and fill the frame. Skip ultra-wide (0.5x) from here, as it will make the bridge look tiny.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 560 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the bridge along the lower or middle third so the curved line leads across the picture. Keep the phone level so the deck does not look as if it slopes. Try one wide frame with some trees or sky for context, and one zoomed frame that fills the picture with the wooden ribs.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the wood keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows or the phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady. Live Photos can help you pick a frame when people walk through the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the wood. After dark, when the ribs are lit, is the time for night shots.

text.access_note: The bridge is part of a public walking trail, but check the official site before you go for any closures or works along the route.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday.
At the default lens (1x) the bridge will look small from about 555 m away.
A wall or railing can be used to steady a phone for night shots.
Other visitors and walkers are likely to pass through the scene at busy times.
